homeMWhPerYear.source: U.S. Energy Information Administration: the average U.S. home used 10,791 kWh of electricity in 2022 (eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=97)

footballFieldAcres.source: NFL Rulebook, Rule 1: a field with end zones is 360 × 160 feet = 57,600 square feet; 1 acre = 43,560 square feet

dcShare2023.source: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report (December 2024): share of total U.S. electricity used by data centers in 2023

dcShare2028.source: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report (December 2024): projected range for 2028

conversationDba.source: CDC, What Noises Cause Hearing Loss? (normal conversation, in A-weighted decibels)

text.K-2: Welcome to the **town council**, {name}! A company wants to build a giant data center here. You get to help decide!
text.3-5: Welcome to the Wilmington **town council**, {name}! A company wants to build a giant data center. Tonight, you decide.
text.6-8: You're on the Wilmington **town council**, {name}. A company has asked to build a huge data center. Tonight you vote.
text.9-12: You sit on Wilmington's **town council**, {name}. A developer has applied to build a hyperscale data center. Tonight: approve, reject, or approve with conditions.

text.K-2: First we'll look at it. Then some neighbors will talk. Then you **vote**!
text.3-5: First, see how big it is. Then hear from five neighbors. Then **vote**.
text.6-8: First size it up, then hear from five neighbors, then **vote**. There's no single right answer.
text.9-12: Size it up, hear public comment, then **vote**. Reasonable people can weigh the same evidence differently.

text.K-2: **Ms. Rivera** works for the schools. She says: “The company will pay taxes. That money could help our school!”
text.3-5: **Ms. Rivera**, from the school board, says: “The company will pay taxes. That money could pay for teachers and books.”

text.6-8: **Ms. Rivera** (school board): “Its taxes could help our schools.” The panel shows a **rough estimate** per student. Tax breaks can change it a lot.
text.9-12: **Ms. Rivera** (school board): “This could grow our tax base.” The per-student figure is a **rough estimate**; tax abatements decide what schools actually get.

text.3-5: **Mr. Okafor** lives near the site. He says: “The cooling fans could be loud at night. I want my home to stay quiet.” The red circle shows where it might be loud.

text.6-8: **Mr. Okafor** (lives nearby): “I'm worried about noise.” A normal conversation is about **{conversationDba} decibels**. Compare the panel's rough estimate.
text.9-12: **Mr. Okafor** (neighbor): “What about noise at night?” Normal conversation is about **{conversationDba} dBA**. The panel's figure at the nearest home is a rough estimate.

text.6-8: **Mrs. Lindqvist** (farmer): “That's {acres} acres we could farm. Once it's paved, it's hard to get back.”
text.9-12: **Mrs. Lindqvist** (farmer): “{acres} acres taken out of farming. Land use is hard to undo.”

text.K-2: **Jamal** builds things for his job. He says: “Building it means lots of jobs for people like me!”
text.3-5: **Jamal** is a builder. He says: “Building it means years of work for people like me. And some people will work there after.”

text.6-8: **Jamal** (construction worker): “Building it means years of work.” Building jobs end when it's done. The panel's **rough estimate** shows long-term jobs.
text.9-12: **Jamal** (construction worker): “Years of work.” Construction jobs end at build-out; the panel's **rough estimate** shows permanent jobs.

text.9-12: **Mr. Chen** (parent, undecided): “Who pays for new power lines? Is there enough water?” The bill change is a **rough estimate**.
